steps: Unpack & inspect
Check the stove and parts for transit damage. Remove the hardware box and the three floor refractory stones from the firebox, and the packaging in the flue collar and above the baffle.

Pack list: stove, owner's manual and hardware kit (4 feet, 4 carriage leveling bolts, 4 hex head mounting bolts, 4 flat washers, 4 lock washers, air control handle and nut, catalyst temperature indicator).

The label hangs on a cable under the stove; don't damage it when lifting. After final positioning it can be stored in the holding clip on the bottom shield.

Report damaged or missing parts to the authorized Hearthstone dealer immediately.
Fit the feet
Lay the stove on its back on a blanket, remove the two shipping brackets and bolt on the four feet with leveling bolts. Stand it up and level.

1. Unbolt the shipping brackets from the pallet; discard the lag bolts.
  2. Lay a blanket behind the stove and confirm the floor refractory stones are out.
  3. Flip the stove onto its back and unbolt the two shipping brackets from the stove.
  4. Fit each foot with one hex head bolt, one flat washer and one lock washer, with the leveling bolt in the bottom of the foot.
  5. Stand the stove on its feet and adjust the leveling bolts.
Feet aren't interchangeable: "A" feet go front-left and back-right; "B" feet go front-right and back-left.
Air handle & catalyst thermometer
Fit the wooden air control handle onto the air control, then install the catalyst temperature indicator. The probe should be spaced 3/8" from the stove body.
Floor protection
On a combustible floor, a continuous non-combustible protector under and beyond the stove: 27-1/2" x 37-1/2" minimum (US). No insulated pad or R-value required.
Clearances
Freestanding room heater only. Take wall and connector clearances from Table 1 / Figure 9 for the pipe type and heatshields used, and check the pipe maker's listing.

Dimensions run from the furthest point on the cast body and are keyed to lettered dimensions A–F defined only in Figure 9, so read them from the page. Optional heatshields reduce them: rear 96-68200, side (single) 96-68205. NFPA 211 wall protection can reduce clearances with approval of the authority having jurisdiction.

Min. alcove ceiling from floor78 1/2"
Canada, single wall pipe18" from the flue to combustibles
Note: p. 9 says not to install the stove into a factory-built fireplace or any fireplace; Table 1 on p. 12 lists a "Fireplace installation" with an 8" mantel/shelf at 61 1/4" from the floor and 7" trim at 13" from the unit.
Outside air (if used)
Kit 96-53400 to a minimum 3" duct (4" adaptor 90-53308), terminated at or below the stove's intake with 1/4" x 1/4" mesh and a hood. Required in mobile homes.
Chimney connector
6" 24 or 25 MSG blued steel, crimped ends toward the stove, three #10 x 1/2" sheet metal screws at every joint including the flue collar. Horizontal runs rise at least 1/4" per foot.

• No aluminum or galvanized steel pipe.
  • Keep the run as short and straight as possible; extra length and elbows add draft resistance and creosote.
  • The connector can't pass through a floor, ceiling, attic, roof space, closet or similar concealed space. Through a combustible wall, use a thimble or pass-through per NFPA 211 or CAN/CSA-B365 (methods A–D on p. 14).
  • Don't install the chimney directly at the appliance outlet; a chimney connector is required.
  • A cleanout tee simplifies chimney cleaning.
Chimney & draft

Listed Type HT (2100° F) chimney per UL 103 / ULC S629 or a code-approved lined masonry chimney, 6" flue, not shared. 3 feet above the roof opening, 2 feet above any roof within 10 feet. Draft -0.06" to -0.1" WC.

• Flue no smaller than the flue collar and no more than three times its cross-sectional area. An existing 8" metal flue can be used with a reducer; masonry maximum 6" round or 8" x 8" tile.
  • Masonry: have a professional inspect it first. Brick or block at least 4" thick, or rubble/stone, always lined (tile with 5/8" wall and 1" air space, or a UL listed 6" stainless liner, insulated or wrapped). The cleanout door must seal.
  • Interior chimney: 2" clearance to combustibles and fire stops at floors and ceilings. Exterior: 1".
  • Recommended height: 16 feet minimum from the top of the stove, 30 feet maximum.
  • Check the draft at installation; above -0.1" WC, install a stovepipe damper.
Mobile home extras
Per 24 CFR Part 3280: outside air kit mandatory, stove fastened to the floor, mobile home chimney & connector kit with spark arrester. Never in a sleeping room.

• Fasten the stove with hold-down clips from the dealer or through the threaded leveling leg hole.
  • Kit (UL103 or CAN/ULC-S629): stainless spark arrester cap, storm collar, adjustable vented flashing 0/12 – 6/12, two 24" chimney pipes, 24" support box with built-in starter section and trim.
  • Chimney at least 3 feet above the roof where it passes and 2 feet above any part of the home within 10 feet; terminations removable at or below 13-1/2 feet above ground without special tools.
  • A chimney exiting 7 feet or less above ground needs a guard up to 7 feet.
  • Remove the chimney when transporting the home. Maintain the structural integrity of walls, floor, ceiling and roof.
Note: p. 14 says not to install the chimney directly at the appliance outlet (a chimney connector is required); p. 20 says that in a mobile home the chimney should be attached directly to the stove.
Break-in fire
The first fire, and the first each season, is a low break-in fire: warm, never hot. Inspect and clean the stovepipe and chimney once break-in is complete.

panels.title: Stove smokes or back-puffs
items: Door opened without prep → open the air fully a minute before; bypass out first
Cold chimney or reverse draft → preheat the chimney; briefly open a window
Blocked, oversized, undersized or short chimney → clean, reline, draft inducer or lengthen
Extra low burn rate or chimney down-draft → burn hotter; fit a chimney cap
More than one appliance on the flue → disconnect the others and seal openings

panels.title: Uncontrolled or short burn
items: Door not sealed or glass gasket leaking → close tightly; replace gaskets
Draft in excess of 0.1 WC → stovepipe damper(s); run at low burn
Extra long or oversized chimney → shorten or reline; damper(s)
High winds or hilltop location → chimney cap

panels.title: Insufficient heat
items: Green or low-Btu wood → air-dried wood, at least one year
Low burn rate → operate at a higher burn rate
Cold exterior or leaky chimney → reline, insulate or replace
Too much heat loss from the house → insulate and seal openings

panels.title: Catalyst faults
items: Fly ash build-up → brush the cold combustor or vacuum lightly
Plugging from wet, pitchy wood or bypass closed before light-off → hot fire, then one hour high
Warping or bowing from long overheating → lower air settings
Not above 500 °F → inspect for damage or plugging; replace if required

light.title: Lighting a fire
light.html:
Use this for everyday fires. The first fire in a new stove, and the first fire each season, should be a gentler break-in fire instead.

  1. Pull the bypass handle out. Open the door and put five or six double sheets of tightly twisted newspaper in the center of the firebox.
  2. Build a tee-pee of about 10 pieces of kindling, 1/2" thick and 10" to 16" long, over the paper.
  3. Open the air control fully by pulling the lever all the way out.
  4. Light the paper. Leave the door slightly open for a moment until the kindling catches and the draft starts to pull, then close it.
  5. Once the kindling is burning, add logs, small ones first. Keep them toward the center, away from the glass.
  6. When the fire is burning well and the catalyst thermometer shows the active range, push the bypass handle in.
  7. Let it run on a high setting for about 20 minutes, then set the air control for the heat you want.
Never use gasoline, lantern fuel, kerosene, charcoal lighter fluid or similar liquids to start or freshen a fire. Don't use a grate: burn directly on the firebox floor.
The stove is hot while it runs. Keep children, pets, clothing and furniture away, and wear fireplace gloves.

breakin.title: Break-in fires
breakin.html:
The soapstone holds natural moisture that has to be driven out slowly, and the furnace cement needs to cure. Firing a new stove too hot can crack the soapstone. Build your first fire, and the first fire every season, like this:

  1. Pull the bypass handle out. Put five or six double sheets of tightly twisted newspaper in the center with about ten pieces of kindling in a crisscross on top.
  2. Open the air control fully, light the paper, and leave the door slightly open for a moment until the draft pulls. Close the door.
  3. Keep a steady, low fire. The stove should get warm, not hot, to the touch. Add a few small chunks of wood at most.
  4. Once it's warm, push the air control all the way in and let the fire die out. Let the stove return to room temperature.
Too hot: visible steam, boiling moisture or hissing means the soapstone is too hot.

Smoke and smells at first are normal

The paints and oils give off some smoke and fumes until the stove is cured, so open a few windows. Early season odors from dust, pet hair or new carpet also fade. If an odor persists, call your dealer.

Cool break-in fires can build creosote quickly and dirty the glass. Look over, and clean if needed, the stovepipe and chimney once break-in is done.

bypass.title: The bypass & catalyst
bypass.html:
A catalytic combustor burns up smoke once it's hot (around 500 °F). The bypass rod decides whether smoke goes through the catalyst or around it. Always move it by its wooden handle.

Rod pulled outbypass open · smoke goes around the catalyst
Rod pushed inbypass closed · smoke goes through the catalyst

Reading the thermometer

  • Inactive: keep the rod pulled out until the stove heats up.
  • Catalyst Active: push the rod in and leave it in while the stove burns in this range.
  • Too Hot: keep the rod pulled out, push the air control fully in, and let the stove cool back into the active range.

Pull the rod out every time before you open the door. With the catalyst working, you should see little to no smoke from the chimney.

Catalyst care

Look at the catalyst at least three times a heating season and brush fly ash or soot off its face with a soft-bristled brush. Work on it only when the stove and ashes are fully cool: lift off the square cook plate on top, pull the bypass out fully, and lift the catalyst from its sled. Put it back, push the bypass in, and replace the plate. Replacement catalysts: part 3050-010 or 3050-020 from your Hearthstone dealer.

burn.title: Air control, burn settings & reloading
burn.html:
The air control lever sits under the ash lip. Pull it toward you for more air and a faster, hotter burn; push it in for a slower, lower burn. It never closes completely.

Lowlever all the way in
Medium lowfrom low, pull out a little less than 1/4"
Medium highfrom low, pull out a little less than 3/8"
Highlever all the way out

Medium low is the typical setting and the one to use when the stove is unattended. A load can last up to 9-1/2 hours on low, but long stretches on low build creosote. Run it on high once or twice a day for 35 to 45 minutes to heat the stovepipe and chimney. The low setting is fixed at the factory and must not be altered.

Reloading

  1. Pull the bypass handle out.
  2. Open the door just a crack, pause, then open it fully so the smoke clears.
  3. Load onto a bed of hot, red coals, keeping wood away from the glass. Close the door.
  4. Run with the air control fully open for 15 to 20 minutes.
  5. Push the bypass in once the thermometer is back in the active zone. After a cool fire or one burned down to coals, that takes about 10 minutes at a medium to high burn.

wood.title: Choosing firewood
wood.html:
Burn only natural firewood (cordwood). Air-dried, seasoned hardwood burns longer, makes better coals and burns cleaner. Seasoned wood is typically at or near 20% moisture; a hand-held moisture meter will tell you.

  • Season green wood: split, stack and let it air-dry for a year. Stack it on skids or blocks and cover only the top; tarps over the sides trap moisture.
  • Log length: up to 18", with 16" recommended.
  • Good choices: the manual's heat-value table ranks hickory, black locust, white oak and apple high, and sugar maple, red oak, white ash and yellow birch medium-high. Aspen, spruce, balsam fir, white pine, basswood and cottonwood rank low.
Never burn garbage or trash, lawn clippings, materials containing rubber (including tires), materials containing plastic, waste petroleum products, paints or paint thinners, solvents, asphalt products, materials containing asbestos, construction or demolition debris, railroad ties, manure or animal remains, paper products (including colored, glossy or gift wrap paper), cardboard, plywood or particleboard, painted, treated, pressure-treated or kiln-dried wood, unseasoned wood, driftwood (including salt water driftwood) or other previously salt-water saturated materials, coal, charcoal, pellets, artificial or wax logs, compressed wood, wood preservatives, metal foils, sulphur, oil, highly volatile fuels or combustibles, or flammable fluids. They can give off toxic or dangerous fumes, make the stove ineffective and cause smoke, and damage the catalyst. Charcoal, pellets, coal, artificial logs or any other material used as fuel are not safe and will damage the catalyst. Burning any fuel other than wood could generate dangerous levels of carbon monoxide in the living space. Using an unauthorized fuel such as coal could produce high levels of carbon dioxide in the living space; at high levels, carbon dioxide could result in personal injury or death. Fire starters made from paper, cardboard, sawdust or wax are fine for lighting.

Keep your woodpile outside the stove's required clearances. Don't load ice-covered wood into a burning stove; the thermal shock can break the glass, soapstone or iron.

ash.title: Removing ashes
ash.html:
Empty the ashes at the end of every week, sooner if they reach the level of the door sill. Ash piled at the door opening can spill out or pack into the gasket channel so the door won't seal.

  1. Let the fire die down or go out completely.
  2. Push any large live coals to the side and remove only the finer ash with a fireplace shovel.
  3. Leave a thin layer of ash in the firebox.

Disposal

  • Put ashes straight into a metal container with a tight-fitting lid and move it outdoors right away.
  • Don't add other trash, and don't pour water into it. Put the lid back on and let the ashes cool.
  • Set it on a noncombustible floor or on the ground outside, well away from anything that can burn, liquid fuels and vehicles. Never set it on a combustible surface or vinyl flooring.
  • Keep the ashes in the closed container until every coal is cold, even if you plan to bury or scatter them.
Never put ashes in wooden or plastic containers, paper or plastic bags, or a trash can with other trash. Coals in a bed of ashes can stay hot for several days.

glass.title: Glass & door gasket
glass.html:
The window is a tough ceramic glass. Clean it only when the fire is out and the glass is cool.

  1. Dip a damp paper towel in gray ash and rub the inside of the glass in circles.
  2. Finish with window cleaner or a stove glass cleaner from your dealer, inside and out.
  3. Wipe it off with a soft cloth or black & white newsprint.
No razor blades, steel wool or abrasives: scratches weaken the glass. Don't run the stove with the glass cracked or broken, and don't slam the door.

Glass that always stays dirty means the fire runs too cool or the wood is wet. A good hot fire burns off residue left by low burns. Replace broken or chipped glass right away with the ceramic glass kit, PN 90-58605, from your dealer.

Note: p. 29 says only a qualified service person should replace the glass panel; the same page says to wear work gloves and safety glasses if you replace the glass yourself.

Door gasket

Every other month, with the stove cool, close the door on a dollar bill. If it pulls out with no resistance, the door isn't sealing: adjust the latch or change the gasket (kit PN 90-58600). Replace the gasket every two to three seasons.

chimney.title: Creosote & chimney fires
chimney.html:
Slow, cool fires leave tar and moisture that condense in the chimney as creosote. Once ignited, it burns extremely hot and can damage the chimney or even destroy the house.

  • Check the chimney connector and chimney at least every two months in the heating season (a mirror through the firebox works). If you find build-up, check at least monthly.
  • Clean the stovepipe right away if more than 1/8" has built up. A certified chimney sweep is recommended.
  • Prevent it: burn with the air fully open for 35 to 45 minutes daily and for 15 to 20 minutes after reloading, and burn dry wood.
  • Before each season, have the whole system professionally inspected and cleaned.

If you have a chimney fire

  1. Alert everyone in the house. If the fire is too threatening, leave and call the fire department.
  2. Close the air control, the bypass (push it in) and any stovepipe damper. Keep the door closed.
  3. If possible, use a dry chemical extinguisher, baking soda or sand. Never use water: it can cause a dangerous steam explosion.

Don't use the stove again until a qualified chimney sweep or fire department inspector has checked the stove and chimney.

safety.title: Safety & over-firing
safety.html:
• The stove is hot whenever it burns. Keep children and pets away, and keep furniture, drapes, clothing and other combustibles at least 36" from it.
  • Keep the space under the stove clear, with no wood stored there and no pets lying there, so the air intakes on the bottom stay open.
  • Keep the door closed except when you light or load it. Never put clothing or candles on a hot stove.
  • Install smoke and carbon monoxide (CO) detectors throughout the heated space: the stove's area, bedrooms, hallways and common areas. The safety list suggests placing a smoke detector away from the stove itself. Test them regularly.
  • Keep a fire extinguisher rated "A B C" handy.

Signs of over-firing

Never over-fire your stove; it damages the stove. Over-firing means running hotter than a normal high burn. Watch for warped parts, short burn times, a roaring sound in the stove or stovepipe, or a discolored stovepipe. Too much draft, the wrong fuel, worn gaskets or a door left open can cause it.

If you suspect over-firing, stop using the stove and call your dealer right away. Any sign of over-firing voids the warranty.

Color changes and small surface fractures in the soapstone are normal. If a panel breaks completely, it must be replaced.

warranty.title: Warranty at a glance
warranty.html:
Hearthstone covers defects in material or workmanship for the original retail purchaser only, when an authorized Hearthstone dealer or their representative installs the stove. It isn't transferable and starts on the original invoice date. "Limited Lifetime" means 10 years.

Stone; cast iron not listed elsewhereLimited Lifetime
Door handles, latches; steel parts and firebox5 years
Refractory, vermiculite panels, baffles2 years
Enamel finish, accessories, glass, other parts1 year

Catalyst: warranted by its maker, Applied Ceramics. It's replaced at no charge if it stops working within two years, then at set prices from $130.00 in year 3 to $160.00 in year 6.

Note: p. 36 gives two (2) years for no-charge catalyst replacement, and also refers to replacements "during the three year period."
Note: the parts grid on p. 37 covers glass for 1 year and refractory, vermiculite panels and baffles for 2 years, but the exclusions on p. 38 call glass, baffles and refractory materials wear parts that aren't covered.

Not covered

  • Damage from over-firing (any sign of it voids the warranty) or from fuels the manual doesn't allow
  • Damage from installing, running or maintaining it other than as the manual and codes say
  • Modifications, or service by anyone other than an authorized dealer

To claim, contact your Hearthstone dealer within the warranty period.

specFloor.title: Floor protection
specFloor.html:
A combustible floor needs a continuous non-combustible protector (tile, brick, slate, glass or other non-combustible facing) under the stove and extending beyond it.

US minimum27-1/2" x 37-1/2"

Insulated hearth pad / R-valuenot required

How far the protector extends past the stove on each side is shown only in Figure 8 on this page. Some LVP and LVT flooring begins to warp at 110° Fahrenheit; check the flooring maker's limits and add shielding if needed.

Note: p. 10 prints the Canadian minimum width as 30 5/8" and 762mm side by side, and those two figures are not the same length.

They're keyed to lettered dimensions A–F defined only in the drawing, so read them from the page. Through-the-wall and alcove rows (p. 12) and connector clearances (Table 3, p. 13) work the same way.

Maker's website: Clearances, single-wall connector, no shields: Side 13.75", Rear 10" (15.25" CAN), Corner 9.5" (12.5" CAN); double-wall connector, no shields: Side 13.75", Rear 9", Corner 9.5"; double-wall connector with heat shields: Side 9", Rear 3.5", Corner 4". Install to the clearance diagrams in the manual.
